comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing as someone living and working lawfully in the United States to urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw the proposed rule eliminating the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364). Claiming that ending this grace period will have a "negligible" impact on families and the U.S. economy shows a complete disconnect from how financial obligations and school systems actually work in this country.

Like hundreds of thousands of skilled visa holders, I have built a lawful, tax-paying life here. We do not live out of suitcases. We finance cars through U.S. banks, pay monthly EMIs, carry auto and home insurance policies, and sign binding 12-month apartment leases or 30-year mortgages. If a company goes through a sudden layoff on a Friday afternoon, how can a worker legally wrap up years of financial commitments by Saturday morning? It takes weeks to get an auto loan payoff quote, clear a vehicle lien, transfer a title at the DMV, close bank accounts, cancel insurance policies, and pack a home. Without a 60-day window, laid-off workers face an impossible choice: stay a few weeks to lawfully sell their car and settle debts—putting them out of status—or abandon financed cars, leases, and mortgages at the airport. When thousands of workers are forced to walk away from active loans and housing contracts overnight, American banks, credit unions, dealerships, landlords, and insurers will absorb billions of dollars in forced defaults. Under Executive Order 12866 and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)), DHS cannot ignore these massive, foreseeable costs to U.S. credit markets.

Even more heartbreaking is what this rule does to children—especially hundreds of thousands of U.S.-born citizen children whose parents are on H-1B, L-1, E, or O visas due to decades-long green card backlogs. If a parent loses their job mid-year, what happens to their U.S. citizen children the next morning? Minor children cannot stay in the U.S. alone without their parents. Eliminating the 60-day grace period forces American citizen children into sudden, de facto exile from their own country within 24 hours.

Pulling a child out of school overnight mid-semester destroys their education and mental health. U.S. citizen children raised in American public schools often do not read or write the local language of their parents' home country, nor can they suddenly adapt to a foreign curriculum mid-year. Many foreign schools do not allow mid-year admissions, meaning these children lose a full school year, lose their friends and support systems without warning, and suffer severe anxiety and trauma. Public Law 105-277 (Section 654) requires agencies to evaluate whether a rule harms family stability and children's well-being. Treating the sudden uprooting of U.S. citizen children as an afterthought violates both that law and basic human decency.

Furthermore, this rule makes job portability under the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) unusable after a layoff. Even if a laid-off worker gets a new job offer the very next day, federal law requires the new employer to obtain a certified Labor Condition Application (LCA) from the Department of Labor before filing an H-1B transfer—taking 7 to 14 business days minimum. With zero grace period, lawful portability after a layoff becomes mathematically impossible.

Finally, forcing laid-off families to scramble into B-1/B-2 visitor status is harsh, unrealistic, and contradicts DHS's claim that this rule reduces USCIS's workload. With zero grace period, a worker laid off at 4:00 PM Friday must gather documents, pay fees, and file Form I-539 to switch to B-2 before midnight that same evening just to stay legal. Worse, filing for B-2 strips away AC21 H-1B portability—meaning when they find a new job weeks later, they cannot start working upon receipt, forcing employers to pay thousands extra in Premium Processing or send them abroad for consular stamping. Meanwhile, USCIS officers will be buried under tens of thousands of emergency I-539 B-2 applications and nunc pro tunc hardship petitions from families just pleading for a few weeks to finish their kids' school term and pay off car loans. If DHS wants to save officer time spent evaluating discretion, the lawful solution under DHS v. Regents of the University of California is to make the 60-day grace period automatic (up to 60 days or the I-94 expiration date, absent fraud or crime), rather than destroying the lives of legal families and U.S. citizen children.

comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern:

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2). I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and preserve this essential protection for employment-based nonimmigrants.

**1. Unexpected Job Loss Should Not Cause Immediate Immigration Instability**

Layoffs, corporate restructuring, budget cuts, and business closures are often beyond an employee's control. Many H-1B and other employment-based visa holders have spent years contributing to the American economy, paying taxes, and complying with immigration laws.

It is unreasonable to expose these individuals to immediate immigration consequences simply because their employer terminates their employment. The existing 60-day grace period provides a limited, reasonable opportunity to find another employer, file an appropriate petition, or pursue another lawful immigration option.

**2. Eliminating the Grace Period Would Harm American Businesses**

Hiring and transferring employment-based nonimmigrant workers requires interviews, internal approvals, immigration counsel, and government filings. Even when employers act promptly, these processes often take weeks.

Removing the grace period would make it substantially harder for American employers to recruit qualified professionals already in the United States. Startups, smaller businesses, research institutions, and technology companies could be particularly affected.

The proposal would also discourage job mobility by increasing workers' dependence on their current employers. This could weaken labor market competition and reduce workers' ability to leave unsuitable or exploitative employment arrangements.

**3. The Proposal Could Increase Administrative Burdens**

Although DHS cites administrative efficiency, eliminating the grace period could create additional costs through emergency immigration filings, consular processing, international travel, and subsequent visa applications.

Employers may face greater legal expenses, recruitment delays, and disruptions to ongoing projects.

DHS should evaluate these indirect costs before eliminating an established regulatory protection. Administrative convenience should not come at the expense of workforce stability and lawful immigration compliance.

**4. The Proposal Disregards Families and Reliance Interests**

Many employment-based nonimmigrants have established homes, signed leases, made financial commitments, and enrolled children in American schools.

Unexpected termination should not force entire families to confront abrupt relocation, educational disruption, or substantial financial losses.

Workers and employers have also made important decisions in reliance on the existing regulatory framework. DHS should meaningfully consider these reliance interests before removing the grace period.

**5. The Current Rule Promotes Lawful Immigration Compliance**

The 60-day grace period does not provide unlimited immigration status or automatic employment authorization. It is a limited, discretionary transition mechanism.

Its purpose is to give workers a reasonable opportunity to comply with immigration requirements after employment ends.

Removing this protection would make compliance more difficult for individuals acting in good faith. A predictable transition period supports an orderly immigration system rather than undermining it.

**6. Less Disruptive Alternatives Are Available**

If DHS believes changes are necessary, it should consider clearer eligibility requirements, simplified documentation, or targeted procedural improvements rather than eliminating the grace period entirely.

The existing 60-day period is already modest. Removing it would impose disproportionate hardship on workers and employers without a sufficiently demonstrated corresponding benefit.

**Conclusion**

The 60-day grace period is a reasonable safeguard that supports American businesses, lawful immigration compliance, workforce mobility, and family stability.

Eliminating it would penalize workers for circumstances beyond their control, increase economic uncertainty, and potentially create greater administrative burdens.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2).

Thank you for considering my comment.

Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Elimination of the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

Agency: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)
DHS Docket No.: USCIS-2026-0364
RIN: 1615-AD22

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders and their dependents.

The existing 60-day grace period is an essential protection for highly skilled foreign workers and their families who contribute significantly to the United States economy.

Losing employment is not always within an employee’s control. Layoffs, company restructuring, budget reductions, project cancellations, and unexpected business decisions can affect hardworking employees without warning. Finding a new employer, completing interviews, negotiating an offer, and having a new employer prepare and file an H-1B transfer petition can take considerable time.

Eliminating the 60-day grace period would create unnecessary hardship for skilled professionals who want to remain in the United States legally and continue contributing to the economy. It could force individuals and their families to leave the country before they have a reasonable opportunity to secure new employment.

This proposal also has a serious impact on H-4 dependents, including spouses and children. Families make long-term commitments in the United States, including housing, education, healthcare, financial obligations, and other responsibilities. An unexpected employment termination should not immediately place an entire family at risk of losing its ability to remain in the country.

The current grace period does not provide an automatic extension of employment authorization or guarantee a new immigration status. It simply provides a limited opportunity for individuals to find another qualifying employer, pursue an appropriate immigration option, change status when eligible, or arrange their departure responsibly.

I respectfully request that USCIS:

1. Retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other affected nonimmigrant classifications.
2. Continue allowing eligible workers reasonable time to find new employment and have a new employer file the appropriate petition.
3. Protect H-4 dependents and other family members from unnecessary immigration hardship resulting from an unexpected employment termination.
4. Consider the financial, emotional, professional, and family consequences before implementing a policy that removes this important protection.
5. If USCIS believes changes are necessary, consider improving the existing process rather than eliminating the grace period entirely.

The United States benefits from attracting and retaining skilled international professionals. Providing a reasonable transition period promotes workforce stability, protects families, supports employers, and allows talented professionals to continue contributing to American businesses and innovation.

I strongly urge USCIS and the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the discretionary 60-day grace period.

comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS,

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed elimination of the existing 60-day discretionary grace period. As an H-1B professional who has invested years of education, hard work, financial resources, and personal sacrifices to build a future in the United States, I am deeply concerned about how this change could directly affect my life.

I came to the United States to pursue my master’s degree. After completing my education, I transitioned from F-1 status through STEM OPT and eventually obtained H-1B employment. Every step required significant financial investment, patience, documentation, and compliance with immigration requirements. I have worked hard to establish my professional career, maintained lawful status, paid taxes, and contributed to my employer and the U.S. economy.

Like many international professionals, I came here with the hope of building a stable career and a secure future. I have made important personal and financial decisions based on that goal.

How this proposal could affect my life:

1. My career and professional future: Losing a job is not always an employee’s choice. Companies restructure, reduce budgets, eliminate positions, and conduct layoffs even when employees perform well. If I unexpectedly lose my job, finding another employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer requires applications, interviews, background checks, an offer, and immigration processing. These steps cannot realistically be completed overnight. Without the 60-day grace period, I could lose the opportunity to continue my career in the United States simply because I did not have enough time to find another employer.

2. My financial stability: I have invested substantial money in my education, relocation, professional development, and establishing my life here. I have ongoing financial responsibilities, including housing, transportation, insurance, and other living expenses. I make financial decisions based on my employment and the expectation that I can continue building my future here. An unexpected termination combined with an immediate loss of a reasonable transition period could force me to abandon financial plans, absorb significant losses, and make rushed decisions about my future.

3. My family and personal life: My life in the United States is not limited to my employment. I have personal responsibilities, family commitments, and long-term plans. If I lose my job, the consequences could extend to my spouse and our future family plans. We could be forced to reconsider where we live, our financial commitments, and our future in this country. It is extremely difficult to build a stable family life when an unexpected employment decision could suddenly put our ability to remain in the United States at risk.

4. The pressure of finding another employer: H-1B workers cannot freely change employers like many other workers. We depend on employers willing to sponsor our immigration status. Finding a suitable position is already challenging, and employers have their own hiring timelines and immigration procedures. Even if I receive an offer, completing the necessary process takes additional time. Removing the grace period would create enormous pressure to find employment immediately, regardless of whether suitable opportunities are available.

5. Years of investment could be disrupted by one unexpected decision: I have spent years studying, developing professional skills, gaining experience, and following the immigration process. I have done what was expected of me to maintain my status and contribute to this country. It would be extremely difficult to accept that an employer’s decision to eliminate my position could force me to leave the country without a reasonable opportunity to continue my career elsewhere. This is not a request for special treatment. It is a request for a fair opportunity to navigate circumstances beyond my control.

My respectful request to DHS:

I understand the government’s responsibility to maintain immigration compliance and program integrity. However, retaining the 60-day grace period does not mean providing unrestricted employment authorization or exempting anyone from immigration requirements. It simply provides a reasonable opportunity to find another qualifying employer, pursue available lawful immigration options, or arrange an orderly departure.

I respectfully request that DHS:
* Consider the real-life consequences of unexpected layoffs and employer-driven terminations.
* Recognize the impact on workers’ financial stability, spouses, children, and long-term family plans.
* Improve administrative processes if necessary rather than eliminating this important protection.

I am commenting from New Jersey as a Software Architect working in the U.S. technology industry.

I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other affected employment-based visa holders.

Expecting skilled professionals and their families to leave the United States immediately after an unexpected job loss is neither practical nor economically sensible.

Please consider the serious consequences:

1. Children’s Education: Many families have children attending American schools and colleges. How can a family suddenly withdraw children from school and college , transfer academic records, arrange admissions in another country, and relocate within 24 hours? This could severely damage children’s education, emotional well-being, and future opportunities.

2. Devastating Financial Losses: Many skilled immigrants have invested their life savings in American homes. Selling a house under extreme time pressure could result in significant financial losses. What happens to mortgages, car loans, retirement accounts, and other financial commitments? These responsibilities cannot be settled overnight.

3. Loss of America’s Skilled Workforce: The United States benefits from experienced software architects, engineers, scientists, researchers, and healthcare professionals. Forcing skilled workers to leave immediately after layoffs could permanently drive valuable talent to competing countries. Replacing that expertise requires time, money, and significant effort.

4. Damage to American Businesses: Sudden departures could disrupt critical technology projects, healthcare systems, research initiatives, and business operations. Companies would face additional recruitment, training, and knowledge-transfer costs.

5. Interruption of Critical Medical Treatment: What happens to families undergoing cancer treatment, major surgeries, pregnancy-related care, or ongoing treatment for serious medical conditions? Abrupt relocation without adequate arrangements could create serious health risks.

6. Economic Consequences: Skilled immigrants contribute to the American economy through federal and state taxes, homeownership, consumer spending, and support for local businesses. Losing these contributors unnecessarily could hurt local economies, reduce tax revenue, and weaken America’s competitiveness.

7. Unfair Consequences of Corporate Layoffs: Employees can lose their jobs because of corporate restructuring, budget cuts, or economic downturns, even when their performance is excellent. Why should an unexpected business decision immediately threaten an entire family’s stability?

8. Damage to America’s Global Reputation: Highly skilled professionals choose the United States because of its opportunities, innovation, and long-term career prospects. Policies that create extreme uncertainty may discourage future talent from investing their careers and families’ futures here.

9. Practical and Legal Challenges: Families need time to secure travel documents, arrange international relocation, terminate leases, manage property, transfer medical records, and resolve employment-related obligations. Immediate departure requirements could make responsible compliance extremely difficult.

My request to policymakers:

Please retain the existing 60-day grace period, for workers facing involuntary job loss. Provide reasonable protections for families with school-age children, individuals undergoing critical medical treatment, and workers actively seeking new employment.

We respect the importance of immigration laws and national security. However, immigration enforcement should also be fair, predictable, economically responsible, and humane.

A job loss should not automatically become a family crisis, an educational crisis, a financial disaster, and a loss of valuable talent for America.

Please reconsider this proposal and its long-term consequences for American families, businesses, and the U.S. economy.

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I request that DHS retain the existing grace period and consider additional protections for employment-based immigrants with approved I-140 petitions, particularly individuals from countries experiencing lengthy green card backlogs, including India.

My primary concerns and recommendations are:

1. Green card backlogs: Indian-born EB-2 and EB-3 workers can remain in temporary H-1B status for many years because of statutory per-country immigrant visa limits. They should not be disproportionately harmed by an unexpected job loss.
2. Approved I-140 protection: DHS should retain the grace period for individuals with approved I-140 petitions who have demonstrated long-term participation in the lawful employment-based immigration process.
3. Long-term lawful residents: Individuals who have lived, worked, paid taxes, and maintained lawful immigration status for more than a decade deserve a reasonable opportunity to transition between employers.
4. Extend protection to 180 days: Rather than eliminating the 60-day period, DHS should consider extending it to 180 days for workers with approved I-140 petitions, especially those affected by lengthy immigrant visa backlogs.
5. Family stability: Dependent spouses and children should not face abrupt disruption of their immigration status, schooling, housing, and family lives because of an unexpected employment termination.
6. U.S.-educated children: DHS should specifically evaluate the impact on children who have spent most of their lives in American schools and may have limited familiarity with their parents’ countries of citizenship.
7. H-1B portability: Eliminating the grace period could make changing employers significantly harder, undermining worker mobility and increasing dependence on a single sponsoring employer.
8. Administrative processing: Employer recruitment, Labor Condition Application certification, legal review, and H-1B petition preparation require time, even when a new employer is willing to sponsor a worker immediately.
9. Economic impact: Sudden departures could disrupt American businesses, reduce tax contributions, create recruitment costs, and affect local communities.
10. Employer accountability: Workers should not feel compelled to tolerate exploitation or avoid reporting violations because losing employment could immediately jeopardize their ability to remain in the country.
11. Reliance interests: DHS should evaluate the expectations of workers and families who have made substantial financial, professional, and educational commitments in reliance on the existing regulatory framework.
12. Less restrictive alternatives: DHS should consider maintaining the 60-day grace period, extending it for approved I-140 beneficiaries, or establishing a separate transition mechanism rather than eliminating protections entirely.
13. Grandfathering: Any final rule should include meaningful transition protections for individuals already maintaining lawful status in the United States.

Final request

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period or revise the proposal to preserve meaningful protections for affected workers and their families.

In particular, I urge DHS to consider a 180-day grace period for approved I-140 beneficiaries experiencing lengthy employment-based green card backlogs.

These individuals have followed the legal immigration process, contributed to the American economy, and established substantial ties to their communities. An unexpected layoff should not erase their ability to pursue lawful employment and permanent residence.

Thank you for considering these comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tapan Doshi
comments.commentText:
Dear DHS and USCIS officials,

I am an H-1B worker, and I strongly oppose the proposal in docket USCIS-2026-0364 to eliminate the discretionary grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I am asking you to withdraw the proposal and keep the existing grace period of up to 60 days.

My wife and I have built a life together in the United States. We have a home in San Jose, friends we see on weekends, and plans for our future. When I read this proposal, I pictured coming home after being laid off and sitting down with my wife at our kitchen table. I would have to tell her I lost my job. Then, in that same conversation, we might have to start figuring out whether we could stay in our home, what we would do with everything in it, and how quickly we would need to leave the country. She would have to make decisions about her own life because of something that happened in a meeting she wasn’t even in.

That is what makes me so angry about this proposal. A company can reorganize, cut a budget, or eliminate an entire team in a single morning. The people losing their jobs may have done everything their employer asked of them. They may have spent years doing work they are proud of. They have no say in when that decision is made, and under this proposal their families could have very little time to respond to it.

Even with the current grace period, finding a new job in time is hard. A hiring manager can want to bring you on and still need weeks for interviews, approvals, and immigration paperwork. Those timelines are largely outside a worker’s control. The grace period gives a willing employer and a qualified worker a chance to complete that process. It also gives families who need to leave time to make arrangements. Think about what that involves in practice. You may need to settle a lease or figure out what to do with your home, get medical records and prescriptions in order, and book travel you had no reason to budget for. Parents may have to explain to their children why they are leaving their school and when they will get to see their friends again. All of this begins while you are still processing the loss of your income.

DHS cites reducing administrative burden as a reason for the change. I ask you to weigh that against the work and expense this proposal would shift onto families. In assessing the costs, please consider how much of a transition depends on other people’s timelines. A prospective employer controls its hiring process. A landlord controls when a lease can be resolved. A family can be doing everything in its power to comply and still need time. The existing rule already gives DHS discretion over the grace period. Please preserve that discretion and the time it can give people to take the next lawful step.

What I want in that moment is very ordinary. I want to be able to sit down with my wife, tell her what happened, and say, “We have some time to figure this out.” I want to be able to call a recruiter, speak with an attorney, and make a decision together about our home and our future. It is deeply upsetting to have to ask the government to leave us that much room after losing a job.

Please withdraw this proposal and preserve the discretionary grace period. Give workers and their families a fair chance to recover from a layoff and make decisions about their lives with some dignity.

To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:
I am submitting this comment to strongly oppose the proposed rule to remove the up to 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers and their dependents under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Restoring the previous policy of zero grace period upon cessation of employment is severely detrimental to the United States economy, global competitiveness, and the basic well-being of legal, highly skilled workers who have followed all immigration laws.
The 60-day grace period was implemented for a practical and economically sound reason: to provide a necessary buffer for talented professionals who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Revoking this rule will have several immediate, negative consequences:
Bullet Loss of Highly Skilled Talent to Competitor Nations: The U.S. relies on nonimmigrant workers (such as those on H-1B, O-1, and L-1 visas) to maintain its edge in technology, healthcare, engineering, and science. Sudden job losses are a normal part of a dynamic labor market. Forcing these workers to immediately depart the country upon termination prevents them from finding new U.S. employers who desperately need their skills, effectively driving top-tier global talent to countries with more predictable and humane immigration systems, like Canada or the United Kingdom.
Bullet Unreasonable Logistical Hardship: Expecting an individual and their family to uproot their entire lives on zero days' notice is logistically impossible. Nonimmigrant workers sign leases, buy cars, enroll their children in American schools, and contribute to local economies. Bullet Chilling Effect on Legal Immigration: The threat of immediate deportation upon unexpected job loss creates a precarious and exploitative environment. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I express my strong opposition to the proposed rule published under Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, which seeks to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) for nonimmigrant workers (including H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E-1, E-2, E-3, and H-1B1 classifications) and their dependent family members.

The existing 60-day grace period is not a loophole; it is a critical administrative safety net that balances executive oversight with basic economic realities. Completely removing this transition window introduces catastrophic personal harm to law-abiding visa holders and creates severe operational friction for U.S. employers.

Below, I outline the critical negative impacts that this proposed rule will inflict on visa holders and their families:

1. Unreasonable Household and Personal Disruption
Nonimmigrant workers construct real lives in the United States. They sign long-term residential leases, pay federal and local taxes, maintain auto loans, enroll their children in U.S. schools, and build community ties. Requiring a high-skilled professional to liquidate bank accounts, break housing contracts, pull children out of school mid-term, and arrange international relocation on the exact day an employment contract ends is logistically impossible and fundamentally unfair. The current 60-day window provides the bare minimum time necessary to execute a humane and orderly departure.

2. Severe Damage to Dependent Spouses and Children (H-4, L-2, E Dependents)
The negative impact of immediate status termination extends far beyond the principal employee. Derivative spouses and children lose their lawful status at the exact second the principal worker’s employment ceases. Spouses holding independent work authorization (such as H-4 EAD or L-2 status) face immediate, sudden job loss, causing double financial harm to a single household and forcing U.S. businesses to abruptly lose two employees instead of one.

3. Complete Destruction of Functional Job Portability
Congress intentionally designed American immigration laws to support job portability so high-skilled talent could pivot to emerging economic needs. Real-world corporate hiring—including multi-stage technical interviews, background checks, Labor Condition Application (LCA) certifications from the Department of Labor, and drafting Form I-129 petitions—routinely takes 3 to 6 weeks. Ending lawful status immediately upon job separation effectively eliminates a laid-off worker's ability to find a new U.S. sponsor, denying domestic companies access to proven talent already inside the country.

4. Vulnerability to Workplace Exploitation and Deterred Whistleblowing
When a worker's continuous right to remain in the country is tied strictly to single-day employment status, the employer gains total leverage. Nonimmigrant workers will become hesitant to report wage theft, dangerous working conditions, uncompensated overtime, or unlawful workplace discrimination out of fear that immediate termination will trigger swift deportation proceedings. The 60-day grace period provides workers with the minimum legal standing required to assert basic labor rights.

5. Unintended Risk of Immediate Deportation Proceedings
DHS acknowledges in its own proposal that eliminating the grace period could lead directly to the issuance of Notices to Appear (NTAs) and the initiation of removal proceedings against individuals whose employment ends unexpectedly. Subjecting lawful, high-skilled professionals—who have committed no crime or immigration violation other than experiencing an unexpected layoff—to removal proceedings places an unwarranted psychological burden on workers and clogs federal immigration courts.

6. Deterioration of American Global Competitiveness
Global talent in artificial intelligence, technology, healthcare, and advanced engineering is highly mobile. Highly skilled foreign nationals choose the United States over international competitors due to regulatory predictability and stability. Removing basic transition buffers sends a signal that the U.S. immigration framework is hostile to foreign talent, driving elite workers toward nations like Canada, the UK, and Australia that offer more stable transition rules.

Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed rule eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I work in the software development industry, and I have seen how competitive and challenging the job market has become for American workers. Qualified American citizens are struggling to find employment, facing lengthy job searches, increased competition, and pressure on wages.

I believe employment-based visas should serve their intended purpose: allowing foreign nationals to work in the United States in connection with specific qualifying employment. If that employment ends, the basis for their employment-related immigration status should end as well, unless they have independently qualified for another lawful status. The visa system should not provide an extended period to remain in the country solely to search for another employer.

I am particularly concerned about the impact of foreign-worker programs on American technology professionals. Employers have access to a large pool of qualified American software developers, yet American workers must also compete with foreign nationals who may be willing to accept lower compensation. I am concerned that this competition can place downward pressure on wages and reduce employment opportunities for American citizens.

While I recognize that this particular proposal does not directly regulate hiring levels or wages, I believe eliminating the 60-day grace period is a reasonable step toward reinforcing the temporary, employment-specific nature of these visa classifications.

American employers should prioritize recruiting and retaining qualified American workers. Our immigration policies should support the domestic workforce and ensure that employment-based visa programs do not unnecessarily disadvantage the citizens those policies are ultimately intended to serve.

I support DHS’s position that the discretionary grace period creates an unnecessary separation between a foreign worker’s immigration status and the qualifying employment on which that status depends.

I respectfully urge USCIS to finalize the proposed rule and eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Removing it would seriously harm families who have built their lives here lawfully.

Layoffs are not about performance. Most U.S. layoffs today come from restructuring, budget cuts, or strategy changes. They rarely reflect employee performance. Many affected workers are top-rated engineers and team leaders. They lose their jobs through no fault of their own. The proposed rule punishes skilled workers for business decisions they cannot control.

We have made the United States our home. Many of us are full-time employees with 15 or more years in this country. We pay high federal, state, and local ,property taxes. We buy homes and cars and invest in our communities. We pay large legal and filing fees for every petition and extension. Many of us have waited years in the green card backlog. We stay, invest because we believe we will one day become permanent residents and citizens. We love USA.

Our children know no other home. Many of our children were born here and are U.S. citizens. Others grew up here from early childhood. They think, speak, and dream as Americans. They are in school, college preparation, sports, and long-term academic projects. These children are America's future. A sudden departure would disrupt their education and harm their mental health. It would also force U.S. citizen children to choose between their parents and their home country.

No family can unwind a life in one day. Without a grace period, a layoff on Monday could mean loss of status the same day. No family can sell a home, settle a mortgage, sell cars, end leases, and withdraw children from school in days. Homes often take months to sell, and forced sales cause heavy losses. Families also face sudden loss of health insurance and costly international moves. The 60-day period gives workers a fair window to find a new employer, change status, or leave in an orderly way.

The mental health cost is real. Workers on temporary visas already live with constant uncertainty. We follow every rule and pay every fee, yet we still have no certainty. Each round of layoffs brings fear for our families. Removing the grace period turns a normal job loss into a family crisis, and big mental ,financial impact.

This rule conflicts with American values. America was built on fairness, opportunity, and respect for families. America has always rewarded hard work and lawful conduct. A humane nation does not treat its lawful, long-term residents as disposable after a business decision.

The rule harms U.S. employers and the economy. The grace period lets U.S. employers hire experienced talent that is already here and productive. Without it, skilled workers must leave, and their knowledge and spending leave with them. Sudden home sales hurt local housing markets. Fewer visa holders will buy homes and cars or spend freely, which slows economic growth. Other countries actively recruit this talent, and this rule would push it elsewhere.

The current rule is limited and fair. The grace period lasts up to 60 days and never goes past the worker's authorized stay. It is discretionary and does not grant work authorization. DHS adopted it in 2017 after public comment, and it has worked for nearly a decade. A job search in today's market often takes the full 60 days, even for highly skilled workers. Reducing administrative burden does not justify the human cost to families. Fairness means giving people reasonable time to respond to sudden changes. Losing status the same day as a layoff gives families no fair chance.

My request. DHS to:

1. Withdraw this proposed rule and keep the 60-day grace period.
2. At minimum, keep the grace period for long-term workers with 10 or more years of lawful U.S. presence, full-time employees, workers with approved immigrant petitions, and parents of U.S. citizen children or of children who have lived here 10 or more years.
We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for basic fairness and time to protect our families from mental and financial trauma after a job loss we did not cause. Respectfully, Thank you for considering this comment.

My family and I own a home in Washington State, where we pay over $14,000 a year in property taxes alone, in addition to federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare and sales tax. We have built our lives here legally and followed every rule. This proposal would let a single layoff, which is almost never the worker's fault, cancel all of that overnight. 1. It punishes workers for employer decisions. Layoffs come from restructuring, market cycles and cost cutting. A worker who did nothing wrong would fall out of status the day the job ends, with no time to find a new employer, sell a home or plan a move. comments.commentText:
I am writing as an AI robotics data annotation specialist and California resident to strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Removing this transition window completely ignores the operational reality of how corporate recruiting, project delivery, and Department of Labor compliance actually function.

From a project delivery perspective, onboarding skilled professionals onto complex enterprise initiatives cannot happen overnight. Even an expedited corporate hiring cycle requires 3 to 4 weeks for interviews, stakeholder alignment, and background screenings. Once an offer is signed, the hiring company must submit a Labor Condition Application (LCA) to the Department of Labor, which takes a statutory 7 business days to certify before a Form I-129 H-1B transfer petition can even be filed with USCIS. Eliminating the 60-day transition period effectively destroys H-1B portability as Congress intended, because no employer can recruit a laid-off professional and clear mandatory federal labor certifications in zero days.

The timing problem is even worse in practice. Most companies do not hire in November and December — hiring freezes, holiday schedules, and year-end budget closures mean a worker laid off in the fall has almost no realistic chance of completing a job search, even within the current 60 days. The truth is that 60 days is already not enough to secure a comparable position in today's market. Rather than eliminating the grace period, DHS should extend it from 60 days to 90 days so the transition window matches how hiring actually works.

DHS has also underestimated the severe financial disruption this rule will inflict on California communities, local businesses, and families. High-skilled visa holders rent and buy homes, finance vehicles, pay substantial state and local taxes, and raise children in California public schools. Forcing a family to break financial contracts and pull children out of school mid-semester due to an unexpected corporate restructuring is both logistically impossible and economically destructive to our local neighborhoods.

Finally, this rule will not achieve its stated purpose of protecting U.S. workers. Jobs are already moving offshore, and workers here are already losing positions to that shift. Eliminating the grace period will not persuade companies to hire more U.S. workers — when a skilled professional is forced to leave the country on short notice, companies will simply move the role offshore with them, and the job leaves America permanently. Keeping experienced professionals in the U.S. workforce keeps the work, the spending, and the tax base here.

Instead of eliminating the grace period altogether, DHS should adopt workable, less burdensome alternatives: (1) extending the current grace period from 60 days to 90 days, (2) granting an automatic bridge of lawful status the moment a new employer files an LCA with the Department of Labor, or (3) providing at least a 90-day transition window for workers with an approved Form I-140 immigrant petition or those with children enrolled in an active K-12 academic term. I strongly urge USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule.

comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Removal of the 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364)
To Whom It May Concern at DHS and USCIS,
I am writing to strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw its proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364).
Currently, I work in the U.S. as a Solution Architect on an H-1B visa, managing day-to-day work for a group of 10 applications for client. Alongside my daily contributions to our technical infrastructure, I am a husband and father. The 60-day grace period under 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2) has provided essential stability for families like mine during unforeseen job transitions or administrative delays.
A Personal Experience with Medical Emergency and Status Transitions
I know firsthand how vital this policy is. Back in 2018, my visa faced an unexpected refusal. At that precise moment, my wife was undergoing intensive treatment for breast cancer—sandwiched directly between chemotherapy, major surgery, and upcoming radiation sessions. Having to resolve complex visa issues while keeping her life-saving medical schedule intact was terrifying. Thanks to the 60-day grace period, I was able to handle these pressing legal and medical matters over a 15-to-20-day span. That short window allowed us to stabilize her care plan before taking next steps.
If this proposed rule had been in place then, my wife would have been forced to interrupt active cancer treatment to leave the country overnight. No family undergoing a health crisis should be subjected to that level of panic.
Impact on Dependent Children in U.S. Schools
Families with dependents in elementary, high school, or college face severe disruption under this proposal. Children who have grown up in local school districts would see their education abruptly cut off mid-semester. Parents who experience sudden employment changes need adequate time to withdraw their children properly, transfer academic records, or transition them to dependent statuses without falling out of compliance.
Logistical Reality of Departure
Ending an employment role and relocating a family internationally involves ending home leases, closing bank accounts, transferring medical records across borders, and booking travel. Expecting families to do this instantly without a grace period is simply unworkable.
The 60-day grace period is a fair, humane, and practical regulatory measure. I respectfully ask USCIS to retain it.
Sincerely,
Shasi

Re: DHS Docket USCIS-2026-0364 — Opposition to Eliminating the 60-Day Grace Period

I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), Docket USCIS-2026-0364. I urge DHS to retain this important protection for employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their families.

I have lived in the United States for more than 14 years. I have built my life here, purchased a home, and established deep roots in my community. After all these years, I consider the United States my home. Like many other workers, I have made long-term financial and personal commitments while living and working here lawfully.

An unexpected layoff is already difficult. Without the grace period, losing a job could also mean facing an immediate crisis involving immigration status, housing, finances, and relocation.

Finding another qualifying employer takes time. Job applications, interviews, offers, background checks, and immigration sponsorship cannot always be completed immediately. The 60-day period gives workers a reasonable opportunity to seek a new position and allows U.S. employers to hire experienced professionals already in the country. Removing it could disrupt hiring and cause employers to lose qualified candidates.

The grace period is just as important when a worker cannot find another job. As a homeowner, I cannot simply leave the country overnight. Selling a home or arranging property management, handling mortgage obligations, closing accounts, and organizing an international move all require planning. I estimate that relocating would cost approximately $10,000, not including potential losses from a rushed home sale or continuing housing expenses. The existing period is limited and discretionary; it does not authorize indefinite residence or employment without authorization. It provides a defined window to pursue eligible immigration options, seek a new sponsoring employer, or prepare to depart in an orderly manner. This supports compliance rather than creating an immediate emergency after an unexpected job loss.

DHS should carefully consider workers’ reliance on the existing rule and the financial consequences for families, U.S. employers, and communities. If DHS has administrative or program-integrity concerns, clearer guidance and documentation requirements would be less disruptive alternatives to eliminating the grace period.

comments.commentText:
Eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders would introduce severe practical, economic, and humanitarian disruptions. Originally codified under the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) regulations to provide stability, this window allows laid-off foreign professionals time to secure a new sponsor, change status, or orderly wrap up their personal affairs.
Removing it is counterproductive for several key reasons:
* **Impossible Logistics for Orderly Departure:** Without a grace period, an unexpected termination instantly pushes a worker out of status the next day. Packing an entire household, terminating leases, selling property, taking children out of school, and booking international travel cannot reasonably happen overnight. Forcing an immediate departure creates artificial unlawful-presence risks for individuals who have consistently followed legal processes.
* **Disruption to U.S. Employers and Critical Industries:** High-skilled hiring takes time—often several weeks to interview, clear background checks, and prepare a Labor Condition Application (LCA) and Form I-129 petition. The 60-day window enables U.S. companies to retain valuable talent that is already vetted and present in the domestic market, rather than losing critical engineers, researchers, and healthcare professionals to competitor nations like Canada or the UK.
* **Increased Vulnerability and Distorted Workplace Dynamics:** Tying legal presence to continuous employment with zero buffer gives employers disproportionate leverage over workers. Employees faced with immediate status violation are far less likely to report labor abuses, safety violations, or unpaid wages out of fear of retaliation and abrupt deportation.
* **Undermining U.S. Global Competitiveness:** The United States relies heavily on attracting the world’s top STEM talent. Making the immigration system more rigid and volatile signals to international professionals that building a career and a life in the U.S. carries high, unmanageable personal risk, deterring top-tier specialists from choosing American firms.
A zero-day policy transforms standard corporate restructuring into an immediate family crisis while hurting domestic business needs. Maintaining the 60-day grace period remains an essential, pragmatic baseline for economic efficiency and basic fairness.

comments.commentText:
Opposition to the Proposed Elimination of the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period – Docket USCIS-2026-0364

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I am an H-1B professional with over six years of experience in data engineering, a master’s degree from a U.S. university, and an approved I-140 immigrant petition. I have followed the lawful immigration process, maintained my employment authorization, paid taxes, and established my career and family in the United States.

I support immigration enforcement and program integrity. However, eliminating the 60-day grace period would create unnecessary hardship for legally employed professionals, their families, and American employers.

1. Unexpected Job Loss Should Not Create an Immediate Immigration Crisis

Layoffs, corporate restructuring, acquisitions, and economic downturns are often beyond an employee’s control. The existing grace period provides limited but essential time to find another sponsoring employer, arrange immigration filings, pursue other lawful options, or prepare for an orderly departure.

Removing this protection would create immediate uncertainty for workers who have complied with immigration laws. An unexpected job loss should not eliminate a reasonable opportunity to pursue lawful alternatives.

2. Impact on Families and U.S.-Citizen Children

I am married and have a young U.S.-citizen child. Like many other legally employed professionals, my family has established a life in the United States.

Unexpected employment termination could force families to make urgent decisions regarding relocation, housing, financial obligations, healthcare, and childcare. These arrangements cannot always be completed immediately.

A reasonable transition period protects family stability without granting indefinite immigration status.

3. Negative Impact on American Employers

The grace period also benefits U.S. businesses by allowing them to recruit experienced professionals already working in the country.

Hiring, interviews, background checks, immigration petition preparation, and employment transitions require time. Eliminating the grace period could increase recruitment costs, disrupt business operations, and make it harder for American companies to retain specialized talent.

In technical fields such as data engineering and cloud computing, replacing experienced employees can be especially challenging.

4. Consideration for Approved I-140 Beneficiaries

Many professionals have completed labor certification and received approved I-140 petitions but remain in temporary status for years because of employment-based immigrant visa backlogs.

I am one of these individuals. An unexpected job loss should not immediately destabilize years of lawful immigration progress.

I also urge DHS to preserve appropriate protections relating to compelling-circumstances employment authorization for eligible approved I-140 beneficiaries.

5. The Existing Grace Period Is Already Limited

The current grace period is discretionary and limited to a maximum of 60 days or the remaining authorized validity period, whichever is shorter. It does not independently authorize employment.

Therefore, retaining it would not undermine immigration enforcement. Instead, it provides a reasonable mechanism for managing unexpected employment transitions.

6. Reasonable Alternatives and Reliance Interests

Rather than eliminating the grace period, DHS should consider clearer eligibility requirements, improved documentation procedures, and streamlined petition processing.

DHS should also carefully evaluate the reliance interests of employers and workers who have made career, housing, financial, and family decisions under the existing regulatory framework.

The economic and human costs of eliminating this protection may outweigh the anticipated administrative benefits.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period and retain the existing protection under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

A fair immigration system should enforce the law while providing reasonable flexibility for individuals who have complied with its requirements.

Preserving this limited protection would support American businesses, protect families, and promote an orderly and lawful immigration process.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the elimination of the 60-day grace period, stating it creates unnecessary hardship.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strongest opposition to the proposed rule that seeks to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders and other nonimmigrant professionals. As an H-1B worker who has built a life, a career, and a family in the United States, I can state unequivocally that removing this grace period will result in an absolute humanitarian and financial disaster for thousands of legal, law-abiding tax-paying families.
The 60-day grace period is not a loophole. It is a critical safety net that recognizes that high-skilled immigrants are human beings with deep ties to their local communities, not just economic units that can be unplugged overnight. Eliminating it ignores the reality of life in the United States and creates an unlivable environment of fear.
I urge USCIS to consider the catastrophic consequences this rule change will have on families and the severe reliance interests it disrupts:
1. Cruelty to Children and School Disruption:
Many H-1B visa holders have children who are enrolled in American schools. Some of these children are U.S. citizens by birth. Others have lived here most of their lives. Forcing a family to depart the country immediately upon a sudden layoff means pulling children out of school in the middle of a semester, abandoning their teachers, peers, and routines within days. Expecting parents to pack up their children’s lives instantly is a profound violation of the principle of child welfare and family unity.
2. Legal and Financial Traps (Leases and Assets):
Living in the United States requires signing legally binding contracts. H-1B families hold long-term residential house leases, car loans, and utility contracts. If a worker is laid off and the grace period is removed, they are placed in a legal paradox, staying to properly break a lease or sell a car will make them unlawfully present, while fleeing the country immediately forces them to breach legal contracts, default on debts, abandon property, and face ruinous financial penalties. A 60-day window is the bare minimum required to legally and responsibly wind down affairs or secure a transfer.
3. Destruction of Personal Finances, Investments, and U.S. Assets:
H-1B workers invest heavily in the American economy. We buy vehicles, maintain bank accounts, pay substantial local and federal taxes, and invest in U.S. financial markets. A sudden, mandatory departure leaves workers with no ability to responsibly manage or liquidate their assets without taking massive financial losses. Furthermore, many workers have outstanding consumer debt (such as auto loans) that would be forced into default, unfairly harming American financial institutions and creditors who will have no way to collect from individuals forced out of the country overnight.
4. Severe Inequity in the Job Market:
Securing a new H-1B employer transfer takes time. Background checks, interview loops, and the filing of a Labor Condition Application (LCA) and Form I-129 take weeks, if not months. Removing the grace period gives laid-off workers zero business days to find an alternative, effectively ensuring that even an exceptionally qualified worker who finds a new job a few days after a layoff will still be penalized with a gap in status.
Conclusion:
The existing 60-day grace period provides a humane, orderly, and necessary buffer. Removing it does not serve the American economy; instead, it actively harms local communities, inflicts trauma on children, forces default on American debts, and drives top global talent away from the United States.
I strongly urge USCIS to withdraw this proposal and maintain the up-to-60-day grace period to preserve the stability of legal immigrant families and the integrity of the American immigration system.

Opposition to Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule that would eliminate the 60-day discretionary grace period currently available to H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN nonimmigrant workers following the cessation of their employment.

Eliminating this grace period would create significant and immediate hardship for lawfully present foreign workers and their families, often through circumstances entirely beyond their control. Layoffs, corporate restructuring, budget reductions, and business closures are realities of today's employment environment. Employees should not face the possibility of immediately losing their lawful immigration status simply because their employer decides to eliminate a position.

The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable and necessary transition period for affected workers to find another employer willing to sponsor them, secure a new employment opportunity, file an appropriate change-of-status application, or make arrangements to depart the United States in an orderly manner. Removing this protection would place an unreasonable burden on individuals and families who have built their lives in the United States while complying with immigration laws and maintaining lawful status.

The consequences extend far beyond the individual employee. Many affected families have lived in the United States for years, purchased homes, paid federal and state taxes, contributed to local communities, and raised children who attend American schools. Their financial commitments, mortgages, children's education, and family stability cannot simply be put on hold because of an unexpected employment termination. Eliminating the grace period could force families into rushed decisions, create financial uncertainty, and potentially jeopardize their ability to remain in or return to the United States.

Furthermore, the discretionary nature of the existing grace period does not mean that the protection lacks value or should be eliminated altogether. Since its introduction in 2017, this provision has offered DHS the flexibility to consider individual circumstances while providing affected workers with a reasonable opportunity to address changes in their employment situations. Administrative considerations should be balanced against the substantial human, economic, and family consequences of eliminating this provision.

This proposed change could also negatively affect U.S. employers and the broader American economy. U.S. companies invest considerable time and resources in recruiting, hiring, training, and sponsoring highly skilled international professionals. Eliminating the grace period would make the U.S. employment-based immigration system less predictable and less attractive to global talent. It could also make it more difficult for employers to retain experienced professionals and fill critical positions.

**I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw this proposed rule.** At a minimum, DHS should retain the existing 60-day discretionary grace period to ensure that lawfully present workers and their families have a reasonable opportunity to navigate unexpected employment disruptions without facing unnecessary immigration consequences.

The United States benefits from the contributions of skilled professionals, their families, and the businesses that employ them. Immigration policies should provide fairness, predictability, and reasonable protections during circumstances beyond an individual's control.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security and USCIS:

I strongly oppose the proposal to remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Eliminating the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days after employment ends is an unreasonable and disproportionate response to administrative concerns. It would punish workers and families for decisions made by employers, including layoffs, closures, and restructuring beyond the worker’s control. DHS should withdraw this proposal and retain the existing rule.

Consider a worker who has maintained lawful status, complied with all applicable requirements, paid taxes, and performed their job responsibly. The employer unexpectedly cuts the position to reduce costs. That worker has not violated immigration law or chosen to stop working. Yet without the grace period, the loss of a paycheck could become an immediate immigration crisis. The worker may need to arrange international travel, leave a home, terminate a lease, manage debt, and disrupt medical care while trying to understand lawful options. The consequences can extend to a spouse and children, including interrupted schooling and the loss of household income or employment authorization. A corporate budget decision should not trigger this cascade of harm.

Finding new employment is not instantaneous. Applications, recruiter screening, interviews, background checks, hiring approvals, and immigration filings can take weeks. Even when a new employer is willing to hire someone immediately, the necessary paperwork may require coordination and time. Removing the grace period would prevent capable workers from pursuing otherwise lawful transitions simply because their former employer made an unexpected decision. It could also force businesses to restart recruitment or lose qualified candidates who would otherwise remain available in the United States.

The existing grace period is already narrow. It is discretionary, limited to at most 60 days or the remaining authorized validity period if shorter, and does not independently authorize employment. It does not erase the rules governing qualifying employment or guarantee approval of an immigration application. It gives eligible workers a brief opportunity to arrange a lawful transition or orderly departure. Treating this limited safeguard as incompatible with immigration integrity confuses reasonable transition time with unrestricted permission to stay.

DHS argues that eliminating the period would strengthen the connection between status and qualifying employment and reduce administrative burden. Those objectives do not justify the human and economic costs. Reviewing termination dates and supporting documentation is a normal part of immigration administration. If verification creates difficulties, DHS could require standardized employer notices, clarify evidence standards, improve filing instructions, or focus discretionary scrutiny on cases involving genuine compliance concerns. Eliminating the protection for everyone, including workers who followed every rule, is a blunt solution to a problem that calls for targeted improvements.

The proposal also risks increasing employers’ leverage over workers. When job loss threatens immediate departure, workers may hesitate to report unfair treatment, negotiate reasonable conditions, or seek other opportunities. It may also discourage American employers from hiring otherwise qualified people whose work authorization can be transferred or renewed through appropriate procedures. A system that obstructs lawful job mobility weakens workforce flexibility rather than protecting it.

DHS should also give substantial weight to the reliance interests discussed in the proposal. Families and employers have planned around the existence of this limited transition mechanism. The costs of emergency relocation, disrupted schooling, lost economic activity, and complex cross-border hiring deserve consideration even when they are difficult to quantify. Administrative convenience should not outweigh foreseeable and potentially severe hardship without clear evidence that less harmful alternatives are inadequate.

Losing a job is not misconduct. It makes no sense to impose immediate immigration consequences on an otherwise compliant worker because a company decides to eliminate a position. The current 60-day grace period is modest, practical, and consistent with responsible compliance. I urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw the proposed elimination of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), retain the existing grace period, and address any legitimate administrative problems through narrowly tailored reforms.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.commentText:
To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, “Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period,” 91 Fed. Reg. 57,807 (Sept. 11, 2026)
I am submitting this public comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B nonimmigrant workers.
I have lived and worked continuously in the United States on an H-1B visa for over 10 years. Throughout this decade, I have strictly abided by all immigration laws, paid taxes, and fully integrated into my community. As a prospective homeowner preparing to make a substantial, long-term financial commitment in the U.S., I am deeply concerned about the severe disruption and instability this rule would cause for law-abiding long-term residents. 

1. Unrealistic Administrative Demands on Workers and Employers
Eliminating the 60-day grace period means that a worker whose employment ceases would instantly fall out of status the next day. In reality, transferring an H-1B petition requires prevailing wage determinations, Labor Condition Applications (LCAs), and complex petition filings—processes that inherently take weeks or months even under expedited conditions. Requiring instantaneous departure or filing upon job separation creates an impossible compliance burden for both skilled professionals and American employers seeking to hire them.

2. Severe Economic Disruption and Uncounted Monetized Costs
In the proposed rulemaking, DHS admits that it did not monetize or estimate the full economic cost of this rule. For long-term H-1B visa holders who are prospective or current homeowners, sudden termination without a grace period forces abrupt asset liquidations, potential mortgage defaults, lease-break penalties, and immediate financial losses. It undermines the stability required to invest in local housing markets and local economies. 
3. Undermining Reliance Interests of Long-Term Residents
For nearly a decade, high-skilled immigrants and U.S. employers have structured their career, housing, and family planning around the discretionary 60-day grace period framework established under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Abruptly stripping away this cushion penalizes long-term workers who have dedicated years to the U.S. economy while following every rule. 

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the 60-day grace period.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

Losing a job is already stressful, especially when it happens unexpectedly due to layoffs or organizational changes. The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable amount of time for workers to find another employer, explore alternative immigration options, or make arrangements to leave the country.

It is important to remember that this grace period does not authorize individuals to work without proper authorization. It simply gives them time to figure out their next steps without being forced into an immediate and potentially life-changing decision.

Many H-1B professionals have spent years building their careers and lives in the United States. They contribute to American businesses, pay taxes, and participate in their local communities. Losing a job should not automatically mean losing the opportunity to continue contributing to this country.

I believe the existing discretionary framework already provides USCIS with sufficient flexibility to handle individual circumstances. Eliminating the grace period entirely would create unnecessary hardship for workers and employers alike.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

I respectfully oppose the proposed removal of the discretionary grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
I ask USCIS to retain the existing grace period of up to 60 days for eligible workers and their dependents following the end of employment.

I am an H-1B worker living in Pennsylvania with my wife and daughter, who hold H-4 status. My wife works legally under an H-4 Employment Authorization Document.
My daughter is currently in 12th grade and plans to begin college in July or August 2027.

An unexpected job loss would affect our entire family. It could disrupt my employment, create uncertainty about my wife’s ability to continue working, and interrupt my daughter’s education during her transition from high school to college. These consequences could result from a layoff or business decision outside our control.

Our household relies on both my income and my wife’s earnings to meet our ongoing expenses.
Our savings are limited, and we are preparing for our daughter’s college expenses next year.
A disruption affecting both incomes could put significant pressure on our ability to cover basic living expenses and preserve the funds needed for her education.

I own a single-family home and a vacant lot, both with outstanding mortgages, and I make monthly payments on both properties. These financial obligations would continue after a job loss. Owning mortgaged property does not mean that we have readily available cash to manage a sudden loss of income or an immediate international relocation. Selling property, settling financial obligations, and arranging a family move take time. A rushed sale could also cause substantial financial losses.

The existing grace period gives eligible families a limited opportunity to seek another qualifying employer, pursue an available immigration option, or prepare to leave the country responsibly. Finding another position involves applications, interviews, hiring decisions, and preparation of immigration filings. These steps depend on employers and other parties and cannot reasonably be completed immediately after employment ends.

For my daughter, an abrupt disruption during her final year of high school or the beginning of college could affect graduation arrangements, college enrollment, and the educational plans she has worked toward. Dependent children have no control over a parent’s employment situation, yet they could experience significant consequences.

I understand that employment-based immigration status carries conditions. I am asking USCIS to preserve a practical transition period that helps families respond to unexpected employment changes while following immigration requirements.

Before removing this protection, please fully consider the combined effects on workers, employed dependent spouses, children, household income, housing obligations, and education. Please also consider the time that prospective employers need to recruit a worker and prepare the necessary filings.

I respectfully request that USCIS retain the existing discretionary grace period of up to 60 days. It gives families like mine a limited but meaningful opportunity to manage an unexpected employment disruption in an orderly and responsible way.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter asks USCIS to retain the existing grace period and explains how removing it would harm their family.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw its proposal to eliminate the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(2), DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22.

I have worked in cloud and network engineering at major U.S. technology companies for more than eight years. I was laid off in September 2025, and more than four months passed before I received my next job offer. My wife and I were raising our toddler in Texas, and I was still waiting for an employment-based green card. After a layoff, those first weeks matter. Families need time to start a job search and make decisions about their future in the United States.

1. Eliminating the grace period would make H-1B job portability harder to use. Under section 214(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, eligible H-1B workers can start a new job after their prospective employer files a qualifying petition. When a layoff comes with little notice, workers may have only days to interview, receive an offer, and have a new employer prepare and file a petition. The grace period gives workers and employers time to complete those steps.
2. DHS’s own analysis shows how many job transitions could be affected. DHS estimates that up to 3,795 workers across the affected visa categories have a new employer file a petition on their behalf during the grace period each year. Most are H-1B workers. DHS also says it cannot estimate how much time grace-period review adds to each adjudication. Before eliminating the grace period, DHS should explain why the administrative savings justify the disruption to workers and U.S. employers seeking to hire them.
3. The remaining provisions offer little practical help after a layoff. The up-to-10-day period under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(1) is tied to the end of an authorized validity period, so it offers no comparable transition when a worker is laid off before that period ends. Under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(c)(4), USCIS can excuse certain late filings in extraordinary circumstances. Workers and employers need a process they can plan around while a job search and hiring process are underway.
4. Families and employers have made plans around the grace period since 2017. A worker’s job loss could immediately affect a spouse or child whose immigration status depends on the worker’s. Families could face urgent decisions about housing and their children’s schooling while also dealing with the loss of income. DHS acknowledges that workers, families, and employers have relied on the rule. In DHS v. Regents of the University of California (2020), the Supreme Court explained that an agency changing policy must assess significant reliance interests and weigh them against competing concerns. In my view, the proposal gives too little weight to the disruption these families and employers would face.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal and retain the current grace period. If DHS proceeds with a change, I ask it to preserve a meaningful transition period after involuntary job loss and specifically evaluate how 30- and 45-day periods would affect families, employers, and USCIS workload before issuing a final rule.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposal to eliminate the grace period, arguing it harms laid-off workers.
